brief.intro: New to this project type? An onshore wind farm is a series of individually-built turbine positions — each with its own deep foundation, tower, nacelle and blades — tied together by underground medium-voltage cabling into a collection substation that exports to the grid. The programme is not one continuous build; it is dozens of near-identical, repeatable turbine-erection cycles running in a rolling sequence across the site, gated by very large mobile cranes and by turbine component delivery. Access roads and crane hardstands must be built and proven for bearing capacity well ahead of each erection, because a turbine crane cannot mobilise onto unready ground. The true finish line is not the mechanical completion of one turbine but grid-code compliance and power-curve verification across the whole array, which depends on the grid operator and cannot be rushed.

scope.name: Site civil & access roads
scope.desc: Heavy-haul access roads, turbine hardstands and laydown areas built to support crane and blade-transport loads.

scope.name: Turbine foundations
scope.desc: Large reinforced-concrete gravity or piled foundations sized for overturning moment, one per turbine.

scope.name: Turbine erection
scope.desc: Tower sections, nacelle and blades lifted and bolted into place by heavy mobile or crawler cranes.

scope.name: Inter-array (collection) cabling
scope.desc: Underground medium-voltage cabling linking each turbine to the collection substation.

scope.name: Collection substation & grid interconnection
scope.desc: Step-up transformers, switchgear and the single point of grid connection.

scope.name: Earthing & lightning protection
scope.desc: Turbine and array earthing grid plus tower lightning-protection down-conductors.

scope.name: SCADA & turbine control
scope.desc: Plant SCADA, turbine controllers, curtailment logic and met-mast integration.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Mechanical completion per turbine, electrical energisation, grid-code compliance and power-curve verification.

must_get_right: It's heavy-lift and weather-led — crane mobilisation and blade lifts are wind-speed limited; a crane-day lost to weather is rarely recoverable on the same turbine.
Roads and hardstands must be proven for bearing capacity ahead of every erection — a late or under-built access road stops the whole erection train.
Foundation cure time is a real, non-negotiable duration — concrete strength gates tower erection, not just calendar days.
Grid interconnection and power-curve verification, not the last turbine's mechanical completion, are the true finish line — track them as a separate critical path.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The turbine-by-turbine erection cycle is modelled as a repeating (linear) sequence, turbine 1 through turbine n, so crane travel and foundation cure between positions are visible in the logic, not hidden inside one lump activity.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil works run a standard or extended single-shift calendar; the turbine erection calendar is gated by the crane manufacturer's wind-speed limits for tower, nacelle and blade lifts, so planned productivity assumes a realistic number of workable crane-days per month for the region. Commissioning runs a 7-day calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs access road → foundation → cure → turbine erection → inter-array cabling → collection substation → grid interconnection → power-curve test. Foundation cure is a hard, non-crashable duration; crane mobilisation and travel time between turbine positions is itself a logic driver, not free time.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: A single main erection crane (or a stated number of crane sets) is assigned per erection front; turbine component supply matches the planned erection rate; land access, easements and abnormal-load transport permits are secured before mobilisation; and wind resource/met data is finalised before controls tuning. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Sites are often remote with limited road infrastructure, so abnormal-load transport permits for tower sections and blades must be secured well ahead of delivery; a specialist erection crew and main crane are typically shared across the whole array and are a hard resource constraint; wet-season ground bearing can restrict access to hardstands and trenching fronts.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: crane weather downtime, abnormal-load transport delay, grid interconnection/utility delay, and adverse ground conditions at foundations. Schedule contingency is held around the erection weather window and before the grid-code compliance test rather than spread thinly across individual turbines.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones — first turbine erected, last turbine erected, commercial operation date) and Level 2 (summary by turbine group) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 per-turbine lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
